url-shortener.title: URL Shortener
url-shortener.tagline: Global short-link platform: ~100:1 read/write, p99 redirect < 20 ms at the edge, durable codes with optional aliases.

requirements.0: Allocate globally unique short codes; support custom aliases with conflict detection.
requirements.1: Redirect hot paths from edge/CDN with p99 < 20 ms in-region; origin path < 50 ms.
requirements.2: Sustain ~100:1 read:write; target 50k writes/s and 5M redirects/s at peak with linear scale-out.
requirements.3: TTL/expiry, soft-delete, and owner-scoped admin APIs without blocking the redirect path.
requirements.4: Async click analytics that never adds latency to redirects; at-least-once event delivery.
requirements.5: Abuse controls: destination allowlist/HTTPS, rate limits on create, malware URL denylist hooks.

0.name: Clients
0.role: Browsers, apps, and partners hitting create + redirect URLs.

1.name: CDN / edge
1.role: Terminates TLS; caches 301/302 responses and shields origin.

2.name: API gateway
2.role: AuthN/Z, WAF, request shaping, and route split write vs redirect.

3.name: Write service
3.role: Validates destinations, allocates codes, enforces alias uniqueness.

4.name: Redirect service
4.role: Read-optimized resolver; cache-aside then durable store; emits analytics async.

5.name: ID allocator
5.role: Snowflake/range-reserved counters → Base62; avoids central hot lock per request.

6.name: Redis cache
6.role: code → destination (+ expiry); TTL ≤ link expiry; negative-cache 404 briefly.

7.name: Links DB
7.role: Sharded primary for mappings; unique(code), unique(alias) where present.

8.name: Analytics bus
8.role: Kafka/Pulsar topic for redirect events; workers aggregate offline.

tradeoffs.0: 301 (CDN-cacheable, weak per-click analytics) vs 302/307 (countable, more origin load).
tradeoffs.1: Hash(URL) codes (stateless, collision handling) vs counter+Base62 (coordination, denser codes).
tradeoffs.2: Cache-aside (simple, stampede risk) vs write-through on create (warmer cache, write amplification).
tradeoffs.3: Global single table vs shard-by-code-prefix (scale vs cross-shard admin queries).
tradeoffs.4: Strong uniqueness on alias (correct) vs eventual uniqueness (faster writes, repair jobs).

lld.dataModel:
Link {
  code           CHAR(8..12) PK          -- Base62; dense
  alias          VARCHAR NULL UNIQUE     -- optional vanity
  destination    TEXT NOT NULL           -- https only after normalize
  owner_id       UUID NOT NULL
  created_at     TIMESTAMPTZ
  expires_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NULL
  revoked_at     TIMESTAMPTZ NULL
}
Cache entry: code → {destination, expires_at} with TTL = min(policy, remaining TTL)
Shard key: hash(code) % N  (alias lookup via global unique index or alias→code map)
lld.api:
POST /v1/links
  body: { destination, alias?, ttl_sec? }
  → 201 { code, short_url } | 400 invalid URL | 409 alias taken | 429 create budget

GET /{code}   (public redirect)
  → 301/302 Location + Cache-Control | 404 | 410 gone

GET /v1/links/{code}   (authz: owner)
  → metadata without mutating counters

DELETE /v1/links/{code}
  → soft-revoke; purge cache; 204

Analytics are NOT on the redirect response path.
lld.execution:
Create: normalize URL → allocate id range locally → Base62 encode → INSERT with
conflict retry on code → optionally SET cache → return.

Redirect: CDN hit? serve. Else Redirect service: GET cache → on miss GET primary
(replica OK if revoked_at is strongly checked on primary for deletes) → SET cache
→ enqueue {code, ts, ua_hash, edge_pop} → return redirect.

Never await analytics. Negative-cache 404 for ~30s to blunt scans.
lld.failures:
Cache flush → origin with bulkhead + request coalescing (singleflight) per code.
Allocator exhaustion → take new range from coordination service; don't block forever.
DB partition outage → fail creates for that shard; redirects may still hit cache/CDN.
Bus down → keep redirecting; spill events to disk buffer with bounded size then sample.
Malware hit on destination → revoke + purge CDN surrogate keys.

rate-limiter.title: Distributed Rate Limiter
rate-limiter.tagline: Multi-tenant quota plane: token-bucket policies, Redis atomicity, and explicit fail-open/closed SLOs.

requirements.0: Enforce per-key quotas (user, API key, IP, route) with burst + sustained rates.
requirements.1: Decision path p99 < 5 ms in-region when Redis is healthy; deterministic Retry-After.
requirements.2: Identical limits across N app replicas — no per-node drift under retry storms.
requirements.3: Policy tiers (free/pro/internal) loaded without redeploying edge services.
requirements.4: Configurable fail-open vs fail-closed per route class when the store is unavailable.
requirements.5: Observability: allow/deny rates, hot keys, and shadow mode for policy rollouts.

0.name: Caller service
0.role: Business API that must be protected before work starts.

1.name: Limiter sidecar / SDK
1.role: Extracts key, cost, and policy id; short-circuits on deny.

2.name: Policy service
2.role: Serves versioned tier configs; supports shadow evaluate.

3.name: Redis cluster
3.role: Atomic token buckets / sliding windows; key TTL bounds memory.

4.name: Lua / atomic op
4.role: Refill + consume in one round-trip; avoids race between GET/SET.

5.name: Local shedder
5.role: Optional process-local token cache for fail-open soft limits.

6.name: Metrics
6.role: Export allow/deny, latency, and Redis errors for SLO burn alerts.

7.name: Admin API
7.role: CRUD policies, purge keys, and emergency global brakes.

tradeoffs.0: Fixed window (cheap, boundary burst) vs sliding log (accurate, heavier memory).
tradeoffs.1: Token bucket (bursty UX) vs leaky bucket (smooth egress, harsher UX).
tradeoffs.2: Central Redis (consistent) vs local-only (fast, under-enforces under fan-out).
tradeoffs.3: Fail-open (availability) vs fail-closed (cost/security) when Redis times out.
tradeoffs.4: Sync check on every request vs async/optimistic + reconcile (risk of overshoot).

lld.api:
check(key, cost, now, policy_id) →
  { allowed: bool, remaining: float, retry_after_ms: int, policy_version }

HTTP mapping (middleware):
  allow → continue
  deny  → 429 + Retry-After: ceil(retry_after_ms/1000)
           + X-RateLimit-Remaining / X-RateLimit-Limit

Admin:
  PUT /v1/policies/{id}  (version bump)
  POST /v1/buckets/purge { key_prefix }
lld.execution:
One Redis EVAL/Lua (or native atomic): load bucket → refill by elapsed →
if tokens < cost then compute retry_after else subtract → persist → return.

Clock: use Redis TIME or enforce NTP; clamp negative elapsed to 0.
Shadow mode: compute decision + metrics but always allow.
Hot keys: optional local token cache with periodic reconcile (bounded overshoot).
lld.failures:
Redis timeout → per-route fail-open (read APIs) or fail-closed (pay/auth).
Clock jump forward → burst of tokens (cap at capacity); jump back → clamp elapsed.
Hot-key concentration → shard key with salt buckets + fair aggregation, or local shedder.
Policy rollout bug → shadow mode + version pin; emergency global brake via Admin API.
Retries without idempotency → amplify cost; clients must honor Retry-After.

job-scheduler.title: Reliable Job Scheduler
job-scheduler.tagline: Delayed/cron/priority work with leases, fencing tokens, DLQ, and horizontally scaled workers.

requirements.0: Enqueue immediate, delayed, and cron-derived jobs with idempotency keys.
requirements.1: At-least-once execution; side effects must be safe under duplicate delivery.
requirements.2: Worker crash recovery via leases + fencing tokens; no double-ack from zombies.
requirements.3: Priority lanes without starving low-priority traffic forever (aging / fairness).
requirements.4: Operational visibility: queued/running/failed, attempt history, payload refs.
requirements.5: Dead-letter after N attempts with operator replay and poison isolation.

1.name: Scheduler
1.role: Promotes due delayed/cron jobs into ready queues.

3.name: Worker pool
3.role: Claims leases, heartbeats, executes handlers, acks or retries.

4.name: Job store
4.role: Canonical Job row: status, attempts, lease, payload_ref.

5.name: Payload object store
5.role: Large blobs off the hot row; immutable per enqueue version.

6.name: DLQ
6.role: Holds exhausted jobs; separate consumer for ops replay.

7.name: Cron expander
7.role: Materializes next fire times without thundering herds.

8.name: Ops console
8.role: Cancel, requeue, inspect attempts, and pause lanes.

tradeoffs.0: At-least-once + idempotent handlers (practical) vs exactly-once (broker+DB coupling).
tradeoffs.1: Pull workers (backpressure-friendly) vs push (lower idle latency, harder overload).
tradeoffs.2: DB-as-queue (transactions) vs dedicated broker (throughput, operational split).
tradeoffs.3: Per-tenant queues (isolation) vs shared lanes (efficiency, noisy-neighbor risk).
tradeoffs.4: Keep payloads in-row (simple) vs object store (scale, extra failure domain).

lld.api:
POST /v1/jobs  { idempotency_key, run_at?, cron?, lane, priority, payload }
  → 202 { id, status } | 200 existing (same key)

GET  /v1/jobs/{id}
POST /v1/jobs/{id}/cancel     → cooperative cancel flag
POST /v1/jobs/{id}/requeue    → ops only

Worker protocol:
  Claim(lease_ms) → job + fencing epoch
  Heartbeat(id, epoch)
  Ack(id, epoch) | Nack(id, epoch, error, retry_at?)
lld.execution:
Scheduler loop: SELECT due scheduled FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED → push ready queue
→ status=ready.

Worker: claim atomically (status ready→leased, set owner/epoch/until) → run handler
→ Ack only if epoch matches → else discard (fenced).

Retry: attempts++ ; backoff = min(cap, base * 2^attempts + jitter) ; status=scheduled.
DLQ when attempts >= max; never auto-delete payload refs.
lld.failures:
Worker death → lease expiry → another worker claims (at-least-once).
Zombie ack after reassign → fencing epoch mismatch drops the ack.
Broker outage → scheduled rows still durable in Job store; scheduler catches up.
Poison payload → DLQ after N; quarantine lane so one tenant can't block others.
Clock skew on run_at → accept small earliness; document TZ for cron in UTC storage.

log-analytics.title: Log Analytics Pipeline
log-analytics.tagline: Multi-tenant ingest → stream → hot index + cold archive, with bounded queries and retention.

requirements.0: Ingest millions of events/s with backpressure to collectors — no silent drop by default.
requirements.1: Full-text + structured filters; p95 interactive query < 3 s on hot windows.
requirements.2: Time-bucket aggregations for dashboards without unbounded cardinality explosions.
requirements.3: Hot/warm/cold tiers; legal hold and per-tenant retention policies.
requirements.4: Tenant isolation on every query path; redact PII fields at ingest when configured.
requirements.5: Exactly-once-ish processing via event_id dedupe + offset commit after durable write.

0.name: Agents
0.role: Host/sidecar collectors; batch, compress, retry with jitter.

1.name: Ingest gateway
1.role: Auth, schema validate, size limits, per-tenant quotas.

2.name: Kafka buffer
2.role: Partitioned by tenant/service; absorbs spikes with lag SLOs.

3.name: Stream processors
3.role: Parse, enrich, redact, route to index vs quarantine.

4.name: Hot index
4.role: Inverted + columnar shards for recent searchable windows.

5.name: Cold object store
5.role: Compressed originals / Parquet for rehydrate and audit.

6.name: Query API
6.role: Tenant-scoped search + aggregations with timeouts and cursors.

7.name: Compactor / tierer
7.role: Rolls shards warm→cold; enforces retention deletes.

tradeoffs.0: Index-everything (fast UX, $) vs sample/schema-on-read (cheap, weaker search).
tradeoffs.1: Pull ingest from agents vs push HTTP (ops model vs spike amplification).
tradeoffs.2: Shared cluster (efficiency) vs per-tenant indexes (isolation, cost).
tradeoffs.3: Sync ack to agent after Kafka (durability) vs after index (higher latency).
tradeoffs.4: Wide events (debuggable) vs strict schemas (predictable cost/perf).

lld.dataModel:
Event {
  event_id UUID, tenant_id, ts, service, severity,
  trace_id?, body JSONB / text, attrs MAP
}
Kafka key: tenant_id|service  (ordering within partition)
Hot shard: time-bucketed index segment (e.g. 1h) with bloom + postings
Cold: s3://…/tenant/dt=…/part-*.parquet  + manifest
Dedup store: LRU/Bloom of recent event_id per tenant (replay window)
lld.api:
POST /v1/events          batch ≤ N KiB, requires event_id each
GET  /v1/search           ?tenant&from&to&q&cursor&limit
GET  /v1/aggregations     ?tenant&from&to&group_by&interval
                          hard timeout + max buckets; 400 on high-cardinality group_by

All reads inject tenant_id from auth context — never from free client input alone.
lld.execution:
Agent → gateway (auth, quota) → Kafka.
Processor: decode → validate schema → redact → dedupe event_id → bulk index hot
→ put compressed raw to cold → commit offset.

Query: parse → rewrite with tenant filter → fan-out to relevant hot shards
(+ cold rehydrate if window demands) → merge → cursor.

Compactor: merge small segments; tier age-out; apply retention deletes to index AND cold.
lld.pseudocode:
function processPartition(p):
  for batch in p.poll():
    out = []
    for e in batch:
      e = validate(e)
      if e is poison: quarantine(e); continue
      e = redact(e, policy[e.tenant_id])
      if dedup.seen(e.tenant_id, e.event_id): continue
      out.append(e)
    hot.bulkIndex(out)                        // retryable
    cold.put(compress(out))
    dedup.remember(out)
    p.commit(batch.offset)                    // only after durability

function search(q):
  assert q.tenant == auth.tenant
  plan = pruneShards(q.from, q.to)
  return merge(deadline=3s, shards.query(plan, q))
lld.failures:
Kafka lag high → autoscale processors; shed non-critical enrichers first.
Hot index red → serve recent from cold rehydrate (degraded) or fail with 503 + Retry-After.
Poison storm → quarantine + circuit break tenant ingest quota.
Cardinality bomb on aggregations → reject group_by; require pre-agg metrics path.
Split brain retention → single policy worker with fencing; never dual deleters.

sim-regression-dashboard.title: Simulation Regression Control Plane

requirements.0: Ingest results from thousands of tests across revisions with idempotent upserts.
requirements.1: Separate new deterministic fails from flakes and known/waived signatures.
requirements.2: Baseline diff per run: introduced / resolved / persistent failures.
requirements.3: Preserve pass/fail even when artifacts are missing; link logs/waves when present.

0.name: CI / sim farm

waveform-compression.title: Waveform Compression Store
waveform-compression.tagline: Lossless value-change compression with chunked indexes for random-access replay at sim scale.

requirements.0: Lossless for 4-state digital (0/1/X/Z); preserve same-time ordering.
requirements.1: Append path fast enough for live sim dumpers; non-blocking readers.
requirements.2: Random-access read(signals, t0, t1) without full-file scan.
requirements.3: Chunk independence: corrupt/partial tail must not poison sealed chunks.
requirements.4: Dictionary reuse across chunks; versioned format with checksums.
requirements.5: Compression ratio targets depend on activity; measure, don’t promise a constant.

0.name: Sim dump probe
0.role: Streams value-change callbacks from the simulator.

1.name: Capture buffer
1.role: Coalesces transitions; applies backpressure to the probe.

2.name: Delta + RLE encoder
2.role: Time deltas, run-lengths, sparse signal updates.

3.name: Dictionary packer
3.role: Maps enums/buses to compact codes; shared per scope.

4.name: Chunk writer
4.role: Seals compressed blocks with snapshot + checksum.

5.name: Sparse time index
5.role: Maps time ranges → file offsets for seek.

6.name: Object / file store
6.role: Durable chunk bytes; immutability after seal.

7.name: Replay reader
7.role: Loads snapshot + replays deltas for requested window.

8.name: Format verifier
8.role: Offline round-trip tests and version migration tools.

tradeoffs.0: Event-based (great for sparse activity) vs sampled (predictable size, loses X/Z nuance).
tradeoffs.1: Larger chunks (better ratio) vs smaller (faster seeks, more index entries).
tradeoffs.2: Shared global dictionary (ratio) vs per-chunk (parallelism, simpler recovery).
tradeoffs.3: Sync index publish with seal (readers never see holes) vs async (higher write FPS).
tradeoffs.4: Single-file layout (simple) vs multi-file shards (parallel dump from many scopes).

lld.api:
Writer:
  open(path, signals)
  append(signal_id, t, value)          // monotonic t per stream
  flush() → seals chunk + publishes index entry
  close()

Reader:
  read(signal_ids, t0, t1) → iterator of (t, signal_id, value)
  validate() → checksum + version checks

Errors: ERR_TIME_ORDER, ERR_UNKNOWN_SIGNAL, ERR_CHECKSUM, ERR_UNSUPPORTED_VERSION
lld.execution:
Probe pushes transitions into capture buffer.
Encoder emits time-deltas + RLE for idle signals; dictionary codes 4-state values.
When chunk bytes or time-span thresholds hit: write snapshot prefix, compress block,
fsync, then append IndexEntry (readers never observe a chunk without index).

Read: binary search index for covering chunk → decompress → seek snapshot →
replay deltas until t1; skip signals not requested.
lld.failures:
Crash mid-chunk → scanner ignores incomplete tail; last sealed index wins.
Checksum mismatch → skip chunk + surface gap; never silent corrupt replay.
Clock non-monotonic from probe → reject append; sim must flush barriers.
Dictionary change mid-file → new dict version + incompatibility window documented.
Reader ahead of writer → only sealed index entries are visible (MVCC-by-immutability).

maestro.title: MAESTRO — Multi-Agent Ticket Resolution
maestro.tagline: A Cadence multi-agent system that helps engineers resolve simulation tickets end-to-end — with people in control at the high-risk steps.
maestro.summary: MAESTRO is a Cadence multi-agent platform for engineering-ticket resolution on Xcelium workflows. It coordinates specialist AI agents under human oversight so tickets move from triage toward a verified fix with clearer handoffs and less repeated context-gathering. Measured on an internal evaluation set, it cut ticket-resolution time by 45% and root-cause-analysis time by 55%. Built with team Mindsmiths for the Cadence AI Buildathon 2026 and selected for trade-secret protection — implementation details stay internal.
maestro.problem: Simulator tickets often bounce across R&D, validation and documentation. Context lives in many places, handoffs re-gather the same evidence, and under pressure important steps get skipped while backlog items age.
maestro.challenge: Coordinate agent assistance across a ticket’s lifecycle without giving up engineer control, without inventing unsupported conclusions, and without publishing proprietary workflow internals.

approach.0: Framed the product as orchestration plus human gates: agents propose and gather evidence; engineers approve risky transitions.
approach.1: Optimized for grounded answers — conclusions tied to retrieved engineering evidence rather than free-form speculation.
approach.2: Designed for everyday IDE use so the assistive flow meets engineers where they already work.
approach.3: Measured outcomes on an internal ticket sample and treated the system as proprietary Cadence IP after Buildathon recognition.

xcelium-ai-agents.title: ChipStack Xcelium AI Agents — Performance & Memory
xcelium-ai-agents.tagline: Multi-agent LLM workflows that profile Xcelium simulations, diagnose runtime and memory bottlenecks, and apply and verify the fixes.
xcelium-ai-agents.summary: A multi-agent LLM system for Cadence ChipStack AI that profiles Xcelium SystemVerilog simulations, diagnoses runtime and memory bottlenecks, and recommends, applies and verifies fixes — compiler flags, RTL recodes, garbage-collection and memory tuning — from an interactive terminal UI. It spans a performance agent, a memory agent, a shared workflow framework and a regression framework: ~37K lines of Python and 650+ tests.
xcelium-ai-agents.problem: Simulation performance and memory work is expert-heavy: engineers read profiler output, correlate hotspots with RTL, choose flags or recodes, then re-run and compare. Early agent versions routed every mechanical step through LLM tool calls, which made them slow — and let reports quote numbers the parser never produced.
xcelium-ai-agents.challenge: Build agents that go from profiler data to a verified fix with no manual steps, while staying fast, grounded in parsed data, resumable across sessions and testable even though no two runs are identical.

approach.0: Built an 8-agent performance pipeline — intake, planning, a parallel compiler-flag audit / hardware clustering / pattern extraction, a 3-tier RTL recode, apply, then re-run and compare.
approach.1: Built the memory agent: heap snapshots and call-stack profiling, peak detection, shared-library attribution with C++ demangling, RTL file-and-line citations, and garbage-collection experiments with before/after comparison.
approach.2: Re-architected both agents deterministic-first: intake, simulation runs and profile parsing moved out of LLM tool loops into Python, keeping the model for reasoning and fallback.
approach.3: Architected a shared framework on the OpenAI Agents SDK: graph-based orchestration of agent nodes, schema-versioned state with checkpoint/resume, strict structured outputs, recovery from malformed JSON and per-node fallback routing.
approach.4: Eliminated hallucinated figures by rendering report numbers in Python and giving the reporting agents no tools, so every number traces back to parsed profile data.
approach.5: Designed a proof-of-concept regression framework that drives the real terminal UI over a pseudo-terminal: one YAML entry per testcase, and a checklist-based LLM judge that compares each report with a reviewed golden.

xcelium-optimization.title: Xcelium Logic Simulator — Performance Engineering
xcelium-optimization.tagline: Low-level optimization work delivering measurable throughput improvements on large real-world workloads.
xcelium-optimization.summary: A multi-quarter performance engineering effort on Cadence's Xcelium logic simulator, focused on profiling-driven optimization, RTL transformations and structured diagnostics for production customer workloads.
xcelium-optimization.problem: Customer designs of increasing scale stress simulator throughput. Even small inefficiencies in hot paths compound across millions of simulation events, costing engineering hours and infrastructure.
xcelium-optimization.challenge: Identify high-leverage bottlenecks across an industrial simulation engine, reason rigorously about runtime behavior, and ship low-risk C++ changes that move the needle on production workloads.

approach.0: Built a reusable C++ performance-analysis library enabling Top-N profiling and structured diagnostics, presented at Cadence India Conference.
approach.1: Used Valgrind, AddressSanitizer and runtime profilers to isolate hotspots in critical simulation paths.
approach.2: Implemented RTL transformations in the Xform Engine that reshape designs into more simulator-friendly forms.
approach.3: Validated improvements against designs from Apple, Google, Samsung and NVIDIA on representative workloads.

algolens.summary: AlgoLens is an interactive algorithm visualizer supporting 60+ algorithms with real-time step-through, deterministic replay, FFmpeg-WASM export, GenAI explanations and rich search.
algolens.problem: Algorithm learning resources tend to be static. Understanding behavior under different inputs, replaying state and exporting visuals for teaching are awkward at best.
algolens.challenge: Build a fluid, accessible, GPU-friendly visualization engine that handles 60+ algorithms with a unified step model, deterministic replay, video export and AI-assisted understanding — held to product-grade quality bars.

approach.0: Designed a step-based execution model with deterministic replay across all algorithms.
approach.1: Built Canvas-based renderers with smooth, reduced-motion-aware animations.
approach.2: Integrated FFmpeg-WASM for in-browser video export of execution traces.
approach.3: Layered GenAI for natural-language explanations and complexity analysis.
approach.4: Implemented exact, fuzzy, phonetic and semantic search for algorithm discovery.
approach.5: Hardened with WCAG 2.1 AA, Sentry, Web Vitals, Playwright, Storybook, Percy and CI quality gates.

regression-triage.title: Xcelium Regression Triage & Regold System
regression-triage.tagline: A ~16K-line system that turns thousands of regression failures into safe, verified actions — regold, filter, waive or escalate.
regression-triage.summary: After a simulator change, regression campaigns return hundreds to thousands of failing test/mode combinations, and each one needs a decision. This ~16K-line system automates triage, regolds, waivers and verification using rule-based classification, TF-IDF clustering, historical learning and an optional LLM review. It has processed 2,120 failures across 79 runs — 73% of them in runs by other engineers.
regression-triage.problem: Every failing test needs one of several actions: update the golden file, add a diff filter, ignore or waive it, repair the workspace, or escalate. The evidence changes from run to run (addresses, PIDs, timestamps, paths), one root cause produces dozens of near-identical failures, and a wrong regold silently blinds the suite to a real defect.
regression-triage.challenge: Automate the decision safely: recognise the same fault across runs, never let a crash or tool error become the new golden, handle modes that compare against different golden files, verify every change per mode and learn from past campaigns — while staying resumable and undoable.

approach.0: Normalised regression and nightly failure lists into test, bank and mode sets, then re-ran each mode in parallel with per-file locks, dry-run, resume and undo.
approach.1: Canonicalised evidence into run-stable signatures by masking addresses, numbers, paths, PIDs and timestamps, so repeats of one fault share a fingerprint.
approach.2: Categorised every failure with rules, a weighted vote over recent runs and saved human corrections, then grouped similar failures with TF-IDF and agglomerative clustering.
approach.3: Gated disposition by class: only diff-class failures can ever reach a golden file — crashes, timeouts and tool errors always go to root-cause analysis.
approach.4: Verified every regold with a per-mode rerun, and emitted diff filters, IGNORE files or waivers where a regold was not the right answer.
approach.5: Added an optional LLM review (JEDAI) that checks each diff against the pending code change and flags tests that must not be regolded — advisory only, it can never relax the gate.

perforce-replay.title: Cross-Stream Perforce Replay
perforce-replay.tagline: Backport a multi-changelist fix to any release stream in one command — syncing only the paths those changelists touch.
perforce-replay.summary: A fix on the development stream usually has to be reproduced on every supported release stream, often as several changelists — the source change, its regolds and a new test. This tooling derives each changelist's source stream, selectively syncs only the paths the changelists touch, merges them in order and reports exactly which files still need a manual resolve, automating multi-CL backports across Xcelium release branches.
perforce-replay.problem: Backports were done by hand, one changelist at a time, in hand-prepared workspaces. Partial client views meant missing paths surfaced one failure at a time, a full sync was too expensive, the origin stream of each changelist was often unknown, and auto-resolve reported one aggregate status that hid the files it declined to merge.
perforce-replay.challenge: Derive every operand from changelist metadata — the origin stream, which paths must exist in the workspace, and the merge order — so the engineer supplies only changelist numbers and a target branch.

approach.0: Detected the source stream of every changelist from its files, so one run can mix changelists from different streams, and printed the map before merging.
approach.1: Built the sync plan from only the files and directories those changelists touch, instead of syncing the whole tree.
approach.2: Repaired workspace faults automatically — extending the client view for out-of-view paths and recovering clobbered writable files — then retried.
approach.3: Merged changelists in ascending order, each from its own stream at its own revision, so any failure points at exactly one changelist.
approach.4: Ran a single auto-resolve at the end and listed the declined files for manual resolve; nothing is ever submitted automatically.
approach.5: Optionally created a disposable target workspace with only the project configuration synced, and reported the teardown command.

postureiq.title: PostureIQ — Real-Time ML Posture Analysis
postureiq.tagline: A 60 FPS computer-vision coaching system that scores exercise form with deterministic feedback loops.
postureiq.summary: PostureIQ is an ML-powered posture and form-coaching system built around real-time pose estimation, temporal smoothing, confidence gating and rep-quality scoring for exercise feedback.
postureiq.problem: Exercise-form feedback is usually delayed, subjective or dependent on a trainer being present. A useful assistant needs to infer pose continuously and provide clear feedback without jitter or false positives.
postureiq.challenge: Maintain real-time capture, inference and rendering while making noisy pose landmarks stable enough for actionable coaching and automated quality scoring.

approach.0: Built a deterministic capture-to-infer-to-render loop with OpenCV and MediaPipe/BlazePose.
approach.1: Added temporal smoothing, Kalman filtering, confidence gating, adaptive thresholds and 3D landmark checks to reduce noisy corrections.
approach.2: Implemented rep-quality scoring around ROM, tempo and symmetry with audio/visual feedback cues.
